                                     PROJECT NO. 58481
 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                    §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §                    OF TEXAS

     TARGA RESOURCES LLC’S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO COMMISSION
                     STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT

       Targa Resources LLC (“Targa”) appreciates the Commission’s and Commission Staff’s
leadership in advancing a comprehensive framework to formalize and standardize large load
interconnection standards under the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561. Targa
welcomes this opportunity to comment on Commission Staff’s Discussion Draft and offers the
following recommendations on the proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”)
§ 25.194. Targa is a leading U.S. midstream energy company that owns, operates, and develops
critical natural gas gathering, processing, and fractionation infrastructure in Texas and across
ERCOT. Targa currently has large load interconnection requests pending or in planning stages.
Ensuring a workable, transparent, and reliable process for large load interconnections is essential
to maintaining service to critical natural gas infrastructure that supports the ERCOT system and
Texas economy.

                          I.     Responses to Commission Staff’s Questions

Question 1: Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the
commission define those parameters?
       Targa respectfully recommends that the Commission refrain from defining parameters for
“substantially similar interconnection requests” by rule and instead rely on interconnecting
utilities’ existing processes, supported by ERCOT coordination, to identify and manage
duplicative requests. Targa works closely with utilities to differentiate between legitimate,
sequenced projects and duplicative requests, and that cooperation has proven effective in practice.
       The proposed rule frames “substantially similar” as a request that, if approved, would cause
the customer to materially change, delay, or withdraw another request. As drafted, the language



                                                1
 would sweep in numerous legitimate, non-duplicative Targa projects that are sequenced for
business and engineering reasons.
         Targa regularly coordinates with utilities to stage multiple similar interconnections and
provides utilities with sufficient information to identify duplicative requests; this process operates
effectively today without Commission-level definitions. A Commission definition risks reducing
flexibility, increasing administrative burden, and capturing benign portfolio management
decisions that are not the target of this rulemaking.
Question 2: Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large
load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what
is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive
information)? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively
sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a
duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?
         Targa supports the Discussion Draft’s approach to protecting competitively sensitive
information and supports allowing anonymization with redisclosure limited to the Commission
and ERCOT. Targa recommends not codifying a prescriptive list of competitively sensitive items,
as utility confidentiality practices, tariffs, and coordination processes provide a practical pathway
to safeguard sensitive data while enabling identification of genuinely duplicative interconnection
requests. In addition, Targa suggests that pre-public announcement information concerning
project locations, sizing, timing, load commissioning schedules, and the involved utility should be
treated as competitively sensitive and protected from public disclosure, with any necessary
exchange limited to the interconnecting utility and ERCOT under appropriate confidentiality
protections.   Targa also supports Texas Industrial Energy Consumers’ (“TIEC”) comments
recommending the addition of language stating that large load customer disclosures are deemed
confidential “proprietary customer information,” subject to the protections in the Commission’s
rules.
Question 3: Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially



                                                  2
 disclosed in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If
only material changes, how should “material change” be defined?
       Targa supports requiring notice only of material changes to previously disclosed
information, rather than “any change.” The Commission should define “material change” to
include changes that reasonably affect planning, modeling, or scoping. Focusing on changes with
meaningful implications for feasibility and timelines will improve administrative efficiency and
keep attention on the factors more relevant to reliability and project readiness. By contrast
requiring notice of “any change,” however minor, would result in unnecessary administrative work
with little improvement to reliability, diverting attention from changes that affect feasibility or
timeline.
Question 4: Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting utility to refund 20%
of a large load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large load customer
meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased energization of its
contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for refund for reaching
milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased energization (e.g., 20% for each
year of operations until the full amount of security is refunded)? If so, how should the
commission standardize the refund?
       Targa recommends clarifying the refund schedule in the Discussion Draft. Rather than a
condition requiring “sustain[ed] operations for five years at the customer’s contracted peak
demand,” which may not align with large customer loads that operate reliably but do not sit at
“peak” continuously, Targa recommends permitting utility-administered, objective load-
achievement criteria and milestone-based refunds during ramp as appropriate. This approach
preserves protection against stranded costs while supporting the capital efficiency necessary to
advance critical infrastructure.
Question 5: Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with
this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?
       At this time, Targa does not take a position on whether additional changes to other
substantive rules are necessary to align with this rulemaking. Targa reserves the right to address
such issues in future filings if needed.



                                                3
                 II.     Comments on Select Provisions of Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194

   A. Align site control standards across 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(2), (e)(2), and (h)(2).
       As drafted, more stringent site control standards for demonstrating site control apply at the
interconnection request, discretionary services agreement, and intermediate agreement stages.
Targa recommends aligning the site control requirements across these stages in 16 TAC
§ 25.194(c)(2), (e)(2), and (h)(2) by using the same language from subsection (c)(2) for
subsections (e)(2) and (h)(2). In practice, large load customers may defer exercising options to
lease or purchase land until later in the development timeline. Phasing out recognition of option
agreements at earlier stages in the interconnection process would be premature, could cause
compliance issues, and would not reflect current practice.
   B. Strike 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)–(5) and (h)(4)–(h)(5) on site-related studies, engineering
       services, and state and local regulatory approvals.
       Subsections (e)(4)–(5) and (h)(4)–(h)(5) would require attestations regarding site-related
studies for water, wastewater, or gas and progress toward obtaining state or local permits (e.g.,
water, air, backup generation, city or county permits). As discussed in Targa’s comments in
Project No. 58480, these provisions should be deleted for three reasons.
       First, neither the Commission, ERCOT, nor electric utilities possess the subject-matter
expertise to determine when it is commercially reasonable for non-electric studies and permits to
be complete or how to evaluate their sufficiency across diverse industries and jurisdictions.
Embedding such judgments in the electric interconnection process invites inconsistent, subjective
determinations and potential disputes.
       Second, non-electric studies and permits can have materially shorter lead times and critical
paths than major electric interconnection facilities and transmission upgrades, which can take four
to seven years to build. Conditioning forecast inclusion on progress in these areas risks creating
an unnecessary bottleneck on factors that do not drive transmission planning timelines, while
providing little incremental assurance about a project’s electric readiness.
       Third, the rule already contains more tailored, electric-system-relevant indicators of
seriousness and viability—site control, study fees, and financial security.         Those are the
appropriate, technology-neutral gatekeepers for interconnection. Removing subsections (e)(4),
(e)(5), (h)(4), and (h)(5) will streamline administration, keep the criteria within the core
                                                 4
 competencies of the Commission, ERCOT, and electric utilities, and better align the rule with
PURA § 37.0561’s purposes.
   C. Strike 16 TAC § 25.194(l), which would allow ERCOT to establish operational
       standards for large load customers.
       Targa respectfully opposes adopting a new protocol-level operational standards regime for
large load customers as a condition of interconnection and continued operation. Imposing ERCOT
“operational standards” on large load customers outside of emergency firm-load shed contexts
would be novel, would impose uncertain compliance costs and risks, and is not supported by
PURA § 37.0561 or Senate Bill 6’s targeted emergency directives.
       Large Load customers are not one-size-fits-all.        Operational characteristics vary by
industry, process, equipment, and season, and can vary materially even at a single site depending
on equipment mix and process states. At existing facilities, particularly where expansions may
exceed 75 MW, adding new technologies or equipment to meet undefined “operational standards”
can be technically infeasible, cost-prohibitive, or unsafe, and could force costly retrofits or
redesigns that do not improve grid reliability. Subjecting all facilities to broad, protocol-level
directives can create unreasonable health, safety, and economic consequences and risks
disconnecting critical infrastructure without clear statutory authority or demonstrated benefit.
Targa’s natural gas operations are integral to system reliability and the Texas economy; ERCOT
should not have discretionary authority to curtail or condition continued operations of such retail
loads based on undefined “operational standards” beyond utility tariffs and emergency directives.
Targa is supportive of TIEC’s comments recommending removal of proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(l).

                                           III.       Conclusion

       Targa supports the Commission’s objective to implement a structured, reliable, and fair
large load interconnection framework under PURA § 37.0561.              Targa respectfully urges
Commission Staff and the Commission to: decline to define “substantially similar interconnection
request” parameters and allow utility-led administration; refrain from codifying what is
competitively sensitive and protect pre-public announcement project data; limit change notices to
defined “material changes”; and clarify and shorten security refund timelines consistent with
objective, utility-administered energization criteria. Targa respectfully urges Commission Staff

                                                  5
 and the Commission to align site control requirements across 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(2), (e)(2), and
(h)(2) by using the same language as subsection (c)(2); remove the proposed attestations regarding
non-electric, site-related studies and state or local permits in § 25.194(e)(4)-(5) and (h)(4)-(5); and
remove ERCOT “operational standards” imposed on retail large load customers outside emergency
contexts.


                                                       Respectfully submitted,




                                                       __/s/ Martina Sittler __________
                                                       Martina Sittler

                                                       Vice President Engineering &
                                                       Construction, Targa Resources

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                   §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                  §                    OF TEXAS

     TARGA RESOURCES LLC’S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO COMMISSION
                     STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT

                                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •    Do not define “substantially similar interconnection request” parameters in rule; allow
      interconnecting utilities to manage duplicative-request screening and verification under
      existing processes.

 •    Do not codify what is competitively sensitive; treat pre-public announcement project data
      (locations, sizing, timing, involved utility) as sensitive and manage disclosures through
      utilities with confidentiality.

 •    Require notice only of “material changes,” defined as changes that reasonably affect
      planning, modeling, or scoping.

 •    Clarify and accelerate security refunds: allow utility-administered, objective energization
      criteria for early refund; remove the five-year “sustained peak” concept and avoid
      standardized long holdbacks.

 •    Align 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(2), (e)(2), and (h)(2) by using the subsection (c)(2) language
      across all stages, preserving options to lease or purchase land through execution of the
      intermediate agreement.

 •    Delete 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)–(5) and (h)(4)–(5) requiring attestations for water,
      wastewater, gas studies, and state and local permits, which fall outside electric-sector
      competencies, do not drive transmission timelines, and provide little to no assurance of
      electric readiness or viability.

 •    Remove ERCOT “operational standards” for large load customers outside emergency firm-
      load shed contexts; such authority is not supported by PURA § 37.0561 and risks
      unreasonable impacts on critical natural gas operations.
